title: From Fearless Nadia to Alpha: How Bollywood Is Finally Building Female Action Franchises
excerpt: As Alia Bhatt's Alpha prepares to become the first female-led entry in YRF's Spy Universe, industry experts examine why Indian cinema has been slower than Hollywood to build big-budget action spectacles around women — and what's changing.
body:
• Alia Bhatt's Alpha, a spin-off from Yash Raj Films' Spy Universe franchise, is set to become Bollywood's first major female-led action franchise entry alongside co-star Sharvari.
  • Indian cinema's franchise model has historically been built around male heroes, with female-led action films largely limited to mid-budget projects like Naam Shabana (₹37 crore) and the Mardaani series.
  • Industry experts say the gap is one of perception rather than audience acceptance, with studios treating female-led action as a riskier bet despite changing audience preferences.
  • From Fearless Nadia in 1935 to modern stars like Taapsee Pannu and Kangana Ranaut, Indian women have been action icons — but rarely at franchise scale.

When Fearless Nadia cracked her whip across Indian screens in 1935's Hunterwali, she proved that audiences would cheer for a woman dispensing justice. Nearly a century later, Bollywood is still figuring out how to build franchise-scale action cinema around its female stars.

Alpha and the Franchise Question

The arrival of Alpha, starring Alia Bhatt and Sharvari as dual protagonists in Yash Raj Films' Spy Universe — the franchise that includes blockbusters like Pathaan and Tiger 3 — marks a watershed moment. It is the first time a major Hindi film franchise has built a standalone entry around female leads, with Bobby Deol cast as the antagonist.

Yet the fact that it took this long tells its own story. Hollywood has spent years building female-led franchise extensions — Wonder Woman, Black Widow, The Hunger Games, Ocean's 8 — that have proven both commercially viable and culturally resonant. Indian cinema's attempts have been more cautious.

"Most major franchises in Hindi films were conceived around male action heroes, so the narrative universe itself was not originally designed to expand through multiple character-led stories."

— Abishek S Vyas, CEO of AVS Entertainment

The History of Bollywood's Action Heroines

India's action heroine tradition runs deeper than most audiences realize. After Fearless Nadia, the 1970s and 80s produced Hema Malini as Inspector Durga Devi Singh in Andhaa Kaanoon and Rekha's iconic revenge thriller Khoon Bhari Maang. Dimple Kapadia's role as a police officer in Zakhmi Aurat (1988) sparked conversations about justice and gender that remain relevant.

The modern era has brought Rani Mukerji's Mardaani series, Taapsee Pannu's spy turn in Naam Shabana (a spin-off from Akshay Kumar's Baby), Anushka Sharma's raw survival thriller NH10, and Kangana Ranaut's stylized Dhaakad. Malayalam cinema pushed boundaries with Lokah Chapter 1: Chandra, a female superhero film. But most of these operated at mid-budget scale.

Naam Shabana earned approximately ₹37 crore at the domestic box office — respectable, but a fraction of the ₹95 crore its parent film Baby collected. The economics have historically worked against female-led action at franchise budgets.

Perception vs. Reality

Industry insiders say the barrier is less about audience appetite and more about how studios evaluate risk.

"The challenge often is one of perception rather than audience acceptance. Studios tend to mount male-led franchise films on much larger budgets because they are seen as safer opening weekend bets."

— Nivedita Basu, producer and director

Film producer Anand Pandit points to the "gendered idea of heroism" that has shaped franchise thinking globally — from James Bond to John Wick to Ethan Hunt, the franchise protagonist has overwhelmingly been male.

But the landscape is shifting. Streaming platforms have broadened distribution, global audiences have demonstrated appetite for women-led commercial cinema, and younger Indian viewers increasingly reject the notion that action belongs to any single gender.

What's Next

Alpha will be the definitive test case. If it performs, it could open the door to a wave of female-led franchise extensions across Indian cinema's expanding universe model. If it doesn't, studios may retreat to safer territory. For the Indian diaspora audience, many of whom have grown up watching both Hollywood's female action heroes and Bollywood's evolving heroines, the film represents a long-overdue convergence of two traditions.
